concept.name: Bernoulli distribution
concept.definition: The probability distribution of a single trial with exactly two outcomes, conventionally 'success' (X = 1) with probability p and 'failure' (X = 0) with probability 1 - p. It is the building block of the binomial distribution, which counts successes across n independent Bernoulli trials.
concept.intuition: It models any one-shot yes/no event: will this trade close in profit, will this coin land heads? Only one number - p - fully describes it.
concept.mechanics: The random variable takes value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability q = 1 - p. Its mean is p and variance is p(1 - p); summing n independent Bernoulli variables with the same p gives a Binomial(n, p) variable.
concept.formula: P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1 - p; E[X] = p; Var(X) = p(1 - p), where p is the success probability.
concept.failure_modes: It only fits single binary trials with a fixed success probability; applying it to sequences requires independence and constant p, both of which often fail in trading (regime shifts, path dependence). It carries no information about magnitude - a 'win' of 1% and 50% are the same event.
concept.misconceptions: A Bernoulli trial is not any two-outcome situation: the probabilities must be fixed and, for sequences, the trials independent - drawing without replacement violates the setup. Also, p = 0.5 is not required; 'binary' does not mean 'fair'.
concept.example: Modeling one trade as a Bernoulli variable with win probability p = 0.55 gives expected value 0.55 and variance 0.2475; a 20-trade win count then follows a Binomial(20, 0.55) distribution.
